claim: Trypanosomes are important disease agents of humans, livestock and cold-blooded species, including fish.
source: Trypanosomes are important disease agents of humans, livestock and cold-blooded species, including fish.
evidence: This is a general statement about trypanosomes supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: The cellular morphology of trypanosomes is central to their motility, adaptation to the host's environments and pathogenesis.
source: The cellular morphology of trypanosomes is central to their motility, adaptation to the host's environments and pathogenesis.
evidence: This statement is supported by established scientific understanding of trypanosome biology.

claim: T. carassii can change direction through a 'whip-like' motion or by swimming backward.
source: Besides the conventional tumbling and directional swimming, T. carassii can change direction through a 'whip-like' motion or by swimming backward.
evidence: This claim is supported by direct observations in the study using high-speed microscopy.

claim: The posterior end of T. carassii can act as an anchoring site in vivo.
source: Further, the posterior end can act as an anchoring site in vivo.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by in vivo observations presented in the manuscript.

claim: This is the first report of a vertebrate infection model that allows detailed imaging of trypanosome swimming behaviour in vivo in a natural host environment.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first report of a vertebrate infection model that allows detailed imaging of trypanosome swimming behaviour in vivo in a natural host environment.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the work, based on the authors' assessment of existing literature.

claim: Trypanosomes infect animals from all vertebrate classes, including warm-blooded mammals and birds as well as cold-blooded amphibians, reptiles and fish.
source: However, trypanosomes infect animals from all vertebrate classes, including warm-blooded mammals and birds as well as cold-blooded amphibians, reptiles and fish (Simpson et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Simpson et al., 2006.

claim: African trypanosomes, such as Trypanosoma brucei, are exclusively extracellular and are continuously exposed to the innate, humoral and cellular immune systems.
source: African trypanosomes, such as Trypanosoma brucei, are exclusively extracellular and are continuously exposed to the innate, humoral and cellular immune systems.
evidence: This is established knowledge about T. brucei biology.

claim: T. brucei has become a textbook example of antigenic variation based on low frequency switches of the expressed variant surface glycoprotein (VSG).
source: T. brucei has become a textbook example of antigenic variation based on low frequency switches of the expressed variant surface glycoprotein (VSG) that dominates the cell surface and allows the population to escape the host adaptive immune system.
evidence: This is well-established knowledge about T. brucei immune evasion mechanisms.

claim: Individual cell survival is favoured by a process that cleans the cell surface of low levels of bound immunoglobulins through endocytosis and degradation.
source: In addition, individual cell survival is favoured by a process that cleans the cell surface of low levels of bound immunoglobulins through endocytosis and degradation (Engstler et al., 2007; Forlenza et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Engstler et al., 2007 and Forlenza et al., 2009.

claim: Trypanosome motility is an integral part of the process of cleaning the cell surface of bound immunoglobulins.
source: Trypanosome motility is an integral part of this process as the hydrodynamic drag on antibody-VSG complexes, caused by the forward swimming motion of the cell, results in accumulation of the complexes at the posterior pole, close to the flagellar pocket, where endocytosis occurs (Engstler et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Engstler et al., 2007.

claim: Motility is essential for successful cell division, immune evasion and development in the host.
source: In addition, motility is essential for successful cell division, immune evasion and development in the host (Broadhead et al., 2006; Griffiths et al., 2007; Ralston et al., 2006; Shimogawa et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: In vitro studies using African trypanosomes have focused on the characterization of qualitative and quantitative parameters of trypanosome morphology and motility.
source: In vitro studies using African trypanosomes have focused on the characterization of qualitative and quantitative parameters of trypanosome morphology and motility and emphasized the ability of trypanosome species to adapt to the various environments of their mammalian hosts (Alizadehrad et al., 2015; Bargul et al., 2016; Heddergott et al., 2012; Krüger and Engstler, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations describing previous in vitro studies.

claim: Detailed analysis of swimming behaviour, morphology and trypanosome-host cell interaction has been restricted to ex vivo conditions.
source: Thus far, detailed analysis of swimming behaviour, morphology and trypanosome-host cell interaction has been restricted to ex vivo, using conditions that best mimic the host environment, for example in blood taken from naïve or infected animals (Bargul et al., 2016; Beattie and Gull, 1997; Engstler et al., 2007; Heddergott et al., 2012; Hemphill and Ross, 1995; Shimogawa et al., 2018; Skalický et al., 2017; Sunter and Gull, 2016; Wakid and Bates, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous ex vivo studies.

claim: It has not been feasible to recreate complex in vivo microenvironments in vitro.
source: It has not been feasible to recreate complex in vivo microenvironments, which, in the case of the vertebrate host, includes the streaming of the blood, vessels with heterogeneous size and endothelium composition, as well as changes occurring during the course of an infection, for example from the onset of anaemia.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limitations of in vitro systems described in the literature.

claim: It remains a challenge to mimic in vitro the dynamic conditions of the crowded and fast-moving bloodstream in which trypanosomes live.
source: It still remains a challenge to mimic in vitro the dynamic conditions of the crowded and fast-moving bloodstream in which trypanosomes live.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limitations of current in vitro methodologies.

claim: Analysis of trypanosome swimming behaviour in vivo, in a vertebrate host environment, is important to fully understand trypanosome biology and pathogenesis.
source: Given the importance of motility for trypanosome survival, analysis of trypanosome swimming behaviour in vivo, in a vertebrate host environment, is important to fully understand trypanosome biology and pathogenesis.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the importance of motility and the limitations of in vitro studies.

claim: Quantitative and qualitative approaches in vivo are hindered by the lack of transparency of mammalian vertebrate hosts.
source: Quantitative and qualitative approaches in vivo are hindered by the lack of transparency of mammalian vertebrate hosts.
evidence: This is a statement about the technical limitations of studying trypanosomes in mammalian hosts.

claim: Using transgenic trypanosomes expressing a luciferase reporter protein it has been possible to monitor overall trypanosome distribution and to quantify total trypanosome load in mice.
source: Nevertheless, using transgenic trypanosomes expressing a luciferase reporter protein it has been possible to monitor overall trypanosome distribution and to quantify total trypanosome load in mice (Burrell-Saward et al., 2015; Capewell et al., 2016; Goyard et al., 2014; McLatchie et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies using luciferase reporter systems.

claim: Fluorescent trypanosomes have been used in vivo to visualize their presence in mouse skin, a possible reservoir of trypanosomes in the late phase of infection.
source: Fluorescent trypanosomes have been used in vivo to visualize their presence in mouse skin, a possible reservoir of trypanosomes in the late phase of infection (Capewell et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Capewell et al., 2016.

claim: Low spatio-temporal resolution and the lack of transparency of deep tissues limits the possibility for qualitative and quantitative analysis of trypanosome swimming behaviour in vivo in mammalian hosts.
source: Although the sensitivity of both systems allows for indirect visualization of trypanosome location or distribution, low spatio-temporal resolution and the lack of transparency of deep tissues limits the possibility for qualitative and quantitative analysis of trypanosome swimming behaviour in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of luciferase and fluorescent reporter systems in mammalian hosts.

claim: Using a combination of multicolour light sheet fluorescence microscopy and high-speed fluorescence microscopy it has been possible to analyse the infection process and swimming behaviour of T. brucei ex vivo, in dissected tissues of the partially transparent tsetse fly vector.
source: Finally, using a combination of multicolour light sheet fluorescence microscopy and high-speed fluorescence microscopy it has been possible to analyse the infection process and swimming behaviour of T. brucei ex vivo, in dissected tissues of the partially transparent tsetse fly vector (Gibson and Peacock, 2019; Schuster et al., 2017; Wang and Belosevic, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies using advanced microscopy in tsetse flies.

claim: To date, no method is available to study with sufficient resolution trypanosome swimming behaviour in vivo in a vertebrate host environment.
source: Nevertheless, to date, no method is available to study with sufficient resolution trypanosome swimming behaviour in vivo in a vertebrate host environment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the review of existing methodologies in the literature.

claim: T. carassii infects a broad range of cyprinid fish.
source: T. carassii infects a broad range of cyprinid fish (Overath et al., 1998)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Overath et al., 1998.

claim: T. carassii is transmitted by blood-sucking leeches (i.e., Hemiclepsis marginata).
source: is transmitted by blood-sucking leeches (i.e., Hemiclepsis marginata) (Lom and Dyková, 1992)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lom and Dyková, 1992.

claim: T. carassii lives extracellularly in the blood and tissue fluids of the fish.
source: and lives extracellularly in the blood and tissue fluids of the fish (Haag et al., 1998; Lom and Dyková, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Haag et al., 1998 and Lom and Dyková, 1992.

claim: T. carassii can establish a long-term infection characterized by polyclonal B cell activation and recurrent waves of parasitaemia, without expression of a uniform VSG-like surface coat.
source: T. carassii can establish a long-term infection characterized by polyclonal B cell activation and recurrent waves of parasitaemia, without expression of a uniform VSG-like surface coat (Agüero et al., 2002; Joerink et al., 2007; Overath et al., 2001; Overath et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations describing T. carassii infection characteristics.

claim: Phylogenetically, T. carassii belongs to the aquatic clade of Trypanosoma, a sister group that diverged from the Trypanosomatid lineage prior to the divergence of the Stercorarian and Salivarian trypanosomes that infect mammals.
source: Phylogenetically, T. carassii belongs to the aquatic clade of Trypanosoma, a sister group that diverged from the Trypanosomatid lineage prior to the divergence of the Stercorarian and Salivarian trypanosomes that infect mammals (Simpson et al., 2006; Stevens, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Simpson et al., 2006 and Stevens, 2008.

claim: Morphologically, T. carassii isolated from fish has a single flagellum that emerges from the flagellar pocket at the cell posterior, is attached to the cell body and extends free at the anterior end, defining the anterior-posterior axis.
source: Morphologically, T. carassii isolated from fish has a single flagellum that emerges from the flagellar pocket at the cell posterior, is attached to the cell body and extends free at the anterior end, defining the anterior-posterior axis.
evidence: This is a description of T. carassii morphology based on established knowledge.

claim: Zebrafish have been used as a model for developmental biology, as well as biomedical and neurobiology research.
source: Zebrafish have been used as a model for developmental biology, as well as biomedical and neurobiology research (Asnani and Peterson, 2014; Blackburn and Langenau, 2014; Cronan and Tobin, 2014; Goessling and North, 2014; Miyares et al., 2014; Nguyen-Chi et al., 2014; Phillips and Westerfield, 2014; Renshaw and Trede, 2012; Schartl, 2014; Torraca et al., 2014; Veinotte et al., 2014; Zon and Cagan, 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by numerous citations to studies using zebrafish as a model organism.

claim: Zebrafish are a fresh water cyprinid fish closely related to many of the natural hosts of T. carassii.
source: and are a fresh water cyprinid fish closely related to many of the natural hosts of T. carassii.
evidence: This is based on established taxonomic knowledge of fish species.

claim: The great advantage of zebrafish is the transparency of the larvae, and of some juvenile and adult stages.
source: The great advantage of zebrafish is the transparency of the larvae, and of some juvenile and adult stages.
evidence: This is established knowledge about zebrafish as a model organism.

claim: Mutant and transgenic zebrafish lines including those marking blood vessels and relevant immune cell lineages are available.
source: Furthermore, mutant and transgenic lines including those marking blood vessels and relevant immune cell lineages are available (Benard et al., 2015; Bertrand et al., 2010; Ellett et al., 2011; Langenau et al., 2004; Lawson and Weinstein, 2002; Page et al., 2013; Petrie-Hanson et al., 2009; Renshaw et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies describing transgenic zebrafish lines.

claim: The transparency of the zebrafish allows high-resolution, real-time imaging of trypanosome movement and host-parasite interaction in vivo, under conditions that exactly represent the natural environment during infection.
source: The transparency of the zebrafish allows high-resolution, real-time imaging of trypanosome movement and host-parasite interaction in vivo, under conditions that exactly represent the natural environment during infection.
evidence: This is an inference about the advantages of using transparent zebrafish for imaging studies.

claim: Trypanosomes can rapidly adapt their swimming behaviour to the heterogeneous host environments.
source: Our observations reveal that trypanosomes can rapidly adapt their swimming behaviour to the heterogeneous host environments.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on in vivo observations.

claim: It was not possible to assign one preferred swimming behaviour to trypanosomes in either the bloodstream, tissues or other body fluids.
source: It was not possible to assign one preferred swimming behaviour to trypanosomes in either the bloodstream, tissues or other body fluids.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on observations throughout the study.

claim: Conditions such as the presence or absence of the blood flow or of red blood cells, the speed of the flow, the size of the blood vessel, the type of endothelium or epithelium lining the vessels or the tissues, as well as the compactness of the tissues, all influenced the swimming behaviour.
source: Conditions such as the presence or absence of the blood flow or of red blood cells, the speed of the flow, the size of the blood vessel, the type of endothelium or epithelium lining the vessels or the tissues, as well as the compactness of the tissues, all influenced the swimming behaviour.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on systematic observations under different conditions.

claim: Up to 96.4% of T. carassii in carp blood could be classified as tumblers.
source: Analysis of the swimming behaviour of trypanosomes in blood of infected carp revealed that up to 96.4% of T. carassii could be classified as tumblers (Figure 1A–B, and Video 1 (00:00 - 45:19 s)).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 1A-B and Video 1.

claim: 3.5% of T. carassii in carp blood behaved as intermediate swimmers.
source: The remaining trypanosomes (3.5%) behaved as intermediate swimmers (Video 1, 00:00 - 45:19 s)
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data and Video 1.

claim: Only 0.1% of T. carassii in carp blood could be classified as persistent swimmers.
source: and only 0.1% could be classified as persistent swimmers (Figure 1A–B and Video 1, 45:19 - 58:03 s).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 1A-B and Video 1.

claim: Persistent swimmers showed an average speed of 32 μm/s and could cover a 'straight-line' distance of up to 418 μm in 20 s.
source: Persistent swimmers showed an average speed of 32 μm/s and could cover a 'straight-line' distance of up to 418 μm in 20 s
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements from the study.

claim: Intermediate swimmers showed a lower average speed of 14 μm/s.
source: whereas intermediate swimmers showed a lower average speed of 14 μm/s (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: The average cell-body length of T. carassii is approximately 23 ± 2.4 μm.
source: Although tumblers did not move any distance greater than their body length (~23 ± 2.4 μm, Figure 1C)
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements presented in Figure 1C.

claim: The speed of displacement of the posterior end of tumblers was 14 μm/s, similar to that of intermediate swimmers.
source: Taking advantage of the spatio-temporal resolution of high-speed videography, the speed of displacement of the posterior end of tumblers was 14 μm/s, similar to that of intermediate swimmers (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements presented in Figure 1B.

claim: Comparison of the movement of freshly isolated trypanosomes kept in either carp serum or culture medium revealed comparable swimming behaviour.
source: Comparison of the movement of freshly isolated trypanosomes kept in either carp serum or culture medium revealed comparable swimming behaviour (Video 1, 00:58 s - 1:15 min).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Video 1.

claim: Culture in medium or serum for a period of up to 2 months did not alter morphology, the proportions of tumblers, intermediate or persistent swimmers.
source: Culture in medium or serum for a period of up to 2 months did not alter morphology, the proportions of tumblers, intermediate or persistent swimmers (data not shown)
evidence: This claim is based on observations made during the study, though the data is not shown.

claim: The swimming behaviour is an intrinsic property of trypanosomes in blood.
source: suggesting that the swimming behaviour is an intrinsic property of trypanosomes in blood.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that culture conditions did not alter swimming behavior.

claim: In freshly drawn blood from infected carp, trypanosomes were observed anchored to red blood cells or to leukocytes.
source: In freshly drawn blood from infected carp, trypanosomes were observed anchored to red blood cells or to leukocytes.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the study.

claim: Attachment of T. carassii to blood cells always occurred through their posterior end leaving the flagellum free to move.
source: Attachment always occurred through their posterior end leaving the flagellum free to move (Figure 2 and Video 2, 00 - 28 s).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 2 and Video 2.

claim: When cultured, trypanosomes could attach to the flask or glass surface through their posterior end.
source: Similarly, also when cultured, trypanosomes could attach to the flask or glass surface through their posterior end (Video 2, 28 - 55 s).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Video 2.

claim: Trypanosomes were observed to alternate between forward and backward swimming.
source: Finally, trypanosomes were also observed to alternate between forward and backward swimming (Video 2, 00:55 s - 1:15 min).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Video 2.

claim: Infection of 5 day-post-fertilization (dpf) zebrafish resulted in an acute infection associated with low survival and high parasitaemia, independent of the infection dose.
source: Infection of 5 day-post-fertilization (dpf) zebrafish resulted in an acute infection associated with low survival (Figure 3A) and high parasitaemia (Figure 3B), independent of the infection dose.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: Zebrafish, similarly to other cyprinid fish, are susceptible to T. carassii infection.
source: This confirms that zebrafish, similarly to other cyprinid fish, are susceptible to T. carassii infection.
evidence: This is an inference based on the successful infection of zebrafish with T. carassii.

claim: When parasitaemia was low, typically early during infection, trypanosomes were most readily detected in small to medium-sized blood vessels with reduced blood flow and a lower density of red blood cells.
source: When parasitaemia was low, typically early during infection, trypanosomes were most readily detected in small to medium-sized blood vessels with reduced blood flow and a lower density of red blood cells, such as the tail tip loop or intersegmental capillaries (ISCs).
evidence: This is a direct observation from in vivo imaging studies.

claim: In the tail tip loop, trypanosomes were dragged passively by the bloodstream along with red blood cells.
source: In the tail tip loop, trypanosomes were dragged passively by the bloodstream along with red blood cells (Figure 4A, Video 3, 0 - 42 s)
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 4A and Video 3.

claim: Trypanosomes in the tail tip loop were seen to either curl or stretch the cell body as well as occasionally propel their flagellum in the same or opposite direction to the blood flow.
source: and were seen to either curl or stretch the cell body as well as occasionally propel their flagellum in the same or opposite direction to the blood flow (Video 3, 00:42 s - 01:57 min)
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Video 3.

claim: Trypanosomes in the tail tip loop were never seen swimming faster than the flow.
source: but were never seen swimming faster than the flow.
evidence: This is a direct observation from in vivo imaging.

claim: In ISCs, trypanosomes were elongated with their flagellum in the opposite direction to the blood flow.
source: In ISCs, trypanosomes were elongated with their flagellum in the opposite direction to the blood flow (Figure 4B, Video 3, 01:57 - 02:49 min)
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 4B and Video 3.

claim: The diameter of the vessel, the speed of the flow and the presence of colliding red blood cells within the ISC, force the trypanosomes to passively move forward in the direction of the flow.
source: the diameter of the vessel, the speed of the flow and the presence of colliding red blood cells within the ISC, force the trypanosomes to passively move forward in the direction of the flow.
evidence: This is an inference based on observations of trypanosome behavior in ISCs.

claim: In larger diameter vessels with a strong blood flow and higher density of red blood cells, detection and description of swimming behaviour was greatly aided by the use of high spatio-temporal resolution microscopy.
source: In larger diameter vessels with a strong blood flow and higher density of red blood cells, such as the cardinal caudal vein (Video 3, 02:49 - 04:11 min) or artery (Video 3, 04:11 - 04:37 min), detection and description of swimming behaviour was greatly aided by the use of high spatio-temporal resolution microscopy.
evidence: This is a methodological observation about the utility of high-speed microscopy.

claim: In large vessels, trypanosomes are dragged passively by the bloodstream, curling among the densely packed red blood cells.
source: In these vessels as well, trypanosomes are dragged passively by the bloodstream, curling among the densely packed red blood cells.
evidence: This is a direct observation from in vivo imaging.

claim: In real-time speed, only the occasional trypanosome was seen to slow down by rolling or bouncing against the vessel in the peripheral cell-free layer.
source: In real-time speed, only the occasional trypanosome was seen to slow down by rolling or bouncing against the vessel in the peripheral cell-free layer (Figure 4C and Video 3, 03:53 - 04:11 min).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 4C and Video 3.

claim: The typical tumbling movement described in vitro was not observed in the fish, except for those locations where the blood flow was highly reduced or absent.
source: In general, the typical tumbling movement described in vitro was not observed in the fish, except for those locations where the blood flow was highly reduced or absent as in sharp turns of the tail tip (Video 3, 04:37 - 05:09 min), and in locations where leukocytes adhering to the endothelium would create a local disturbance of the flow rate allowing trypanosomes to tumble (Video 3, 05:09 - 05:24 min).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Video 3.

claim: In cases where the blood flow was temporarily interrupted, trypanosomes were able to swim directionally, repeatedly invert direction, or tumble.
source: For example, in cases where the blood flow was temporarily interrupted, trypanosomes were able to swim directionally, repeatedly invert direction, or tumble (Figure 5A, and Video 4, 0 - 01:23 min).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 5A and Video 4.

claim: In cases where the blood flow continued but red blood cells were occluded, trypanosomes were able to persistently swim against the blood flow.
source: In cases where the blood flow continued but red blood cells were occluded, trypanosomes were able to persistently swim against the blood flow (Figure 5B, and Video 4, 01:23 - 02:13 min).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 5B and Video 4.

claim: Trypanosomes could often be seen attached to the endothelium on the dorsal luminal side of the cardinal caudal vein.
source: In addition to being dragged passively within blood vessels, trypanosomes could often be seen attached to the endothelium on the dorsal luminal side of the cardinal caudal vein (referred to as caudal vein, Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from in vivo imaging shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Despite the strong blood flow, attachment (anchoring) could last for several seconds.
source: Remarkably, despite the strong blood flow, attachment (anchoring) could last for several seconds (Video 5, 0 - 01:11 min)
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Video 5.

claim: Anchoring involved a small area of the posterior end of the trypanosome, leaving the cell body and the flagellum free to move.
source: and involved a small area of the posterior end of the trypanosome, leaving the cell body and the flagellum free to move (Video 5, 01:11 - 01:59 min).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Video 5.

claim: Although anchoring could be observed already at 1 dpi, it was more easily detected at later stages of the infection.
source: Although anchoring could be observed already at 1 dpi, it was more easily detected at later stages of the infection.
evidence: This is a direct observation about the timing of anchoring during infection.

claim: Trypanosomes were also seen crawling along the vessel wall involving the entire cell body.
source: Anchoring was not the only mode of attachment, trypanosomes were also seen crawling along the vessel wall involving the entire cell body (Figure 6B, and Video 5, 01:59 - 02:38 min).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 6B and Video 5.

claim: Within blood vessels, anchoring occurred exclusively at the dorsal side of the caudal vein, whereas crawling could occur anywhere in the vein.
source: Within blood vessels, anchoring occurred exclusively at the dorsal side of the caudal vein, whereas crawling could occur anywhere in the vein.
evidence: This is a direct observation about the spatial distribution of different attachment behaviors.

claim: No attachment or crawling was observed in arteries or capillaries, independently of the speed of the blood flow.
source: No attachment or crawling was observed in arteries or capillaries, independently of the speed of the blood flow.
evidence: This is a direct observation about where attachment does not occur.

claim: T. carassii attaches to host cells through their posterior end, both in vitro and in vivo, leaving the flagellum free to move.
source: Altogether, our observations show that T. carassii attaches to host cells through their posterior end, both in vitro (Video 2) and in vivo, leaving the flagellum free to move
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on observations throughout the study.

claim: The posterior end acts as an anchoring site.
source: and suggest that the posterior end acts as an anchoring site.
evidence: This is an inference based on the consistent observation of posterior-end attachment.

claim: A characteristic of T. carassii infections is extravasation from blood vessels into surrounding tissues and tissue fluids.
source: A characteristic of T. carassii infections is extravasation from blood vessels into surrounding tissues and tissue fluids (Haag et al., 1998; Lom and Dyková, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Haag et al., 1998 and Lom and Dyková, 1992.

claim: In zebrafish, extravasation was observed at 1 dpi.
source: In zebrafish, this was observed at 1 dpi
evidence: This is a direct observation from the infection experiments.

claim: In the peritoneal and heart cavities, the swimming behaviour was similar to that observed in vitro, where the majority of the trypanosomes were tumblers.
source: In these environments, the swimming behaviour was similar to that observed in vitro (Video 1 and Figure 1), where the majority of the trypanosomes were tumblers (Figure 7 and Video 6, 0 – 42 s).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 7 and Video 6.

claim: In a field of view of more than 100 trypanosomes in the peritoneal cavity, only three persistent swimmers could be identified.
source: In a field of view of more than 100 trypanosomes in the peritoneal cavity, only three persistent swimmers could be identified (Figure 7B and Video 6, 00:42 s - 01:35 min).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative observations shown in Figure 7B and Video 6.

claim: Trypanosomes were seen anchored by their posterior end to cells of the peritoneal membrane in a manner similar to that observed in the caudal vein.
source: Furthermore, trypanosomes were seen anchored by their posterior end to cells of the peritoneal membrane in a manner similar to that observed in the caudal vein (Video 6, 34 - 42 sec).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Video 6.

claim: In tissues, there was no apparent consistency in swimming behaviour, and trypanosomes alternated between directional and non-directional swimming depending on the compactness of the tissue.
source: Next, we analysed the swimming behaviour of T. carassii in tissues: the tail tip, fins, muscle and interstitial space lining the blood vessels. Here, we observed no apparent consistency in swimming behaviour, and trypanosomes alternated between directional and non-directional swimming depending on the compactness of the tissue.
evidence: This is a summary of observations made in various tissue types.

claim: In the compact tissue of the fins, most trypanosomes were directional swimmers.
source: For example, in the compact tissue of the fins, most trypanosomes were directional swimmers (Figure 8A–B)
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 8A-B.

claim: Swimmers in the fins moved at an average speed of 47.5 μm/s, covering up to 187 μm.
source: Swimmers moved at an average speed of 47.5 μm/s, covering up to 187 μm, before disappearing from view or colliding with an obstacle that resulted in a change in direction (Video 7, 0 – 47 s).

claim: In vivo, backward swimming was only observed in the fins.
source: In vivo, backward swimming was only observed in the fins.
evidence: This is a direct observation about the spatial restriction of backward swimming.

source: Backward swimming was previously observed in vitro or ex vivo for T. brucei motility mutants or for wild type trypanosomes swimming in high-density medium or in whole blood (Bargul et al., 2016; Baron et al., 2007; Branche et al., 2006; Engstler et al., 2007; Heddergott et al., 2012; Shimogawa et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Backward swimming was observed ex vivo for procyclic and mesocyclic stages of T. brucei parasites swimming in confined spaces within the midgut of the tsetse fly.
source: and ex vivo for procyclic and mesocyclic stages of T. brucei parasites swimming in confined spaces within the midgut of the tsetse fly (Schuster et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schuster et al., 2017.

claim: The observation of T. carassii swimming in zebrafish tissues is the first report of backward swimming in a vertebrate host environment.
source: The observation of T. carassii swimming in zebrafish tissues is the first report of backward swimming in a vertebrate host environment.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the finding based on comparison with existing literature.

claim: In the interstitial space lining the cardinal blood vessels, trypanosomes swim directionally or tumble.
source: In the interstitial space lining the cardinal blood vessels (artery and vein), trypanosomes swim directionally or tumble (Video 8, 0 - 23 s)
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Video 8.

claim: Trypanosomes can use the space between cells to pin themselves and effectively invert swimming direction in a 'whip-like' motion.
source: but can also use the space between cells to pin themselves and effectively invert swimming direction in a 'whip-like' motion, a movement distinct from the more random tumbling movement. (Video 8, 00:23 s - 01:17 min).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Video 8.

claim: The 'whip-like' motion combines the swing of the flagellum along one plane, accompanied by a 180°C rotation of the cell body along a third axis.
source: The 'whip-like' motion combines the swing of the flagellum along one plane, similar to the movement of tumblers on a glass surface (Video 1), accompanied by a 180°C rotation of the cell body along a third axis.
evidence: This is a detailed description of the whip-like motion based on observations.

claim: The whip-like motion is possible only in vivo where the cylindrical form of a capillary or interstitial space within a tissue allow the very flexible trypanosome cell body to move in three dimensions.
source: This is indeed possible only in vivo where the cylindrical form of a capillary or interstitial space within a tissue allow the very flexible trypanosome cell body to move in three dimensions.
evidence: This is an inference about why the whip-like motion is observed in vivo but not in vitro.

claim: In compact tissues that do not present a ready passage for trypanosomes, the persistent swimming translates into a drilling (auger) movement.
source: Furthermore, in compact tissues that do not present a ready passage for trypanosomes, the persistent swimming translates into a drilling (auger) movement, which in some cases can lead to an enlargement of the space between somatic cells (Figure 8D, Video 8, 02:18 - 03:52 min).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 8D and Video 8.

claim: In tissues and tissue fluids T. carassii can adopt all swimming movements and can adhere through the posterior end to endothelial cells of the peritoneal cavity.
source: Altogether, in tissues and tissue fluids T. carassii can adopt all swimming movements and can adhere through the posterior end to endothelial cells of the peritoneal cavity.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on observations throughout the study.

claim: Besides the previously described tumbling and directional (forward) swimming, trypanosomes were also able to invert direction through a 'whip-like' motion or by backward swimming.
source: Besides the previously described tumbling and directional (forward) swimming, trypanosomes were also able to invert direction through a 'whip-like' motion or by backward swimming.
evidence: This is a summary of novel swimming behaviors observed in the study.

claim: Non-infected larvae have a strong and steady blood flow, with all blood vessels packed with red blood cells.
source: Non-infected larvae have a strong and steady blood flow, with all blood vessels packed with red blood cells (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is a direct observation of control fish shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Infected larvae progressively showed a decrease in the ratio between red blood cells and trypanosomes from 1 to 8 dpi.
source: In contrast, infected larvae progressively showed a decrease in the ratio between red blood cells and trypanosomes from 1 to 8 dpi (Figure 9B–C)
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 9B-C.

claim: In some cases red blood cells disappeared completely.
source: until in some cases red blood cells disappeared completely (Figure 9D and Video 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 9D and Video 9.

claim: Anaemia is a hallmark of late stages of T. carassii infection in zebrafish larvae.
source: Anaemia, therefore, is a hallmark of late stages of T. carassii infection in zebrafish larvae.
evidence: This is an inference based on the progressive loss of red blood cells during infection.

claim: Highly infected fish that are anaemic also showed vasodilation, a clinical sign typical of advanced stages of infection (>3 dpi) with T. carassii.
source: Highly infected fish that are anaemic also showed vasodilation, a clinical sign typical of advanced stages of infection (>3 dpi) with T. carassii (Figure 10A–C)
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 10A-C.

claim: Vasodilation was most obviously observed in the caudal vein.
source: most obviously observed in the caudal vein.
evidence: This is a direct observation about where vasodilation is most prominent.

claim: In extreme cases, the diameter of the caudal vein could be up to three times larger than that of control fish.
source: The degree of vasodilation differed between individuals, and in extreme cases, the diameter of the caudal vein could be up to three times larger than that of control fish (Figure 10D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 10D.

claim: Vasodilation also occurs in the caudal artery but to a lesser extent.
source: Vasodilation also occurs in the caudal artery but to a lesser extent (not shown).
evidence: This is a direct observation, though the data is not shown.

claim: While the dilated blood vessels of larvae are packed with trypanosomes and have limited circulation, the number of extravasated trypanosomes is very low.
source: Interestingly, while the dilated blood vessels of larvae are packed with trypanosomes and have limited circulation, the number of extravasated trypanosomes is very low (Video 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Video 9.

claim: Knowledge of trypanosome-host cell interaction, movement, and tropism in vertebrate hosts is important to understand trypanosome biology and pathology.
source: Knowledge of trypanosome-host cell interaction, movement, and tropism in vertebrate hosts is important to understand trypanosome biology and pathology.
evidence: This is a general statement about the importance of the research area.

claim: Current in vitro approaches could not fully reproduce the streaming nature of the blood, the heterogeneity of the bloodstream between and within vessels, the different sizes of blood vessels, the different types of endothelium, and the changes that occur in the blood caused by the infection itself.
source: Although the current in vitro approaches have brought a wealth of information on the quantitative aspects of trypanosome motility and potential immune evasion strategies, they could not fully reproduce the streaming nature of the blood, the heterogeneity of the bloodstream between and within vessels, the different sizes of blood vessels between which trypanosomes regularly alternate, the different types of endothelium lining arteries and veins and, finally, the changes that occur in the blood caused by the infection itself.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of in vitro systems based on the complexity of the in vivo environment.

claim: More than 90% of T. carassii in carp blood could be classified as tumblers, independent of whether they were in whole blood, diluted in serum or culture medium.
source: Based on previously proposed descriptions of the swimming behaviour of salivarian trypanosomes in mouse blood (Bargul et al., 2016; Shimogawa et al., 2018), clearly more than 90% of T. carassii could be classified as tumblers, and this was independent of whether they were in whole blood, diluted in serum or culture medium.
evidence: This is a summary of quantitative observations from the in vitro experiments.

claim: The observations are in agreement with a previous study reporting that directional persistent swimming was not a prominent feature of T. brucei in whole blood from an immunocompetent infected mouse.
source: Our observations are in agreement with a previous study reporting that directional persistent swimming was not a prominent feature of T. brucei in whole blood from an immunocompetent infected mouse (Shimogawa et al., 2018)
evidence: This is a comparison with findings from a cited study.

claim: The observations are in contrast to the study by Bargul and colleagues in which up to 30% persistent swimmers and 45% intermediate swimmers could be observed in blood films from immunosuppressed infected mice.
source: but are in contrast to the study by Bargul and colleagues in which up to 30% persistent swimmers and 45% intermediate swimmers could be observed in blood films from immunosuppressed infected mice (Bargul et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a comparison with findings from a cited study.

claim: Differences in T. brucei strains, host immune status as well as the use of whole blood or blood films may account for the observed discrepancies.
source: Differences in T. brucei strains, host immune status as well as the use of whole blood or blood films may account for the observed discrepancies.
evidence: This is speculation about possible reasons for differences between studies.

claim: Both previous studies could not reproduce the streaming of the blood and thus the observations were made under static conditions.
source: Nevertheless, both studies could not reproduce the streaming of the blood and, thus, the observations were made under static conditions.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of the cited studies.

claim: The initial in vitro observations led to the suggestion that the tumbling behaviour might be an intrinsic property of T. carassii in the bloodstream.
source: Our initial in vitro observations led to the suggestion that the tumbling behaviour might be an intrinsic property of T. carassii in the bloodstream.
evidence: This is an inference based on the in vitro observations.

claim: The subsequent in vivo observations showed that tumbling applies only to trypanosomes swimming in fluids with highly reduced or absent flow.
source: However, our subsequent in vivo observations showed that this applies only to trypanosomes swimming in fluids with highly reduced or absent flow, for example the peritoneal fluid or blood in vessels in which the flow was slow or absent (Figure 7A and Video 9).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on in vivo observations that contradicts the initial inference.

claim: Analysis of the swimming behaviour of T. carassii in the zebrafish bloodstream revealed that it is not possible to assign a single or predominant swimming behaviour.
source: In contrast, analysis of the swimming behaviour of T. carassii in the zebrafish bloodstream revealed that it is not possible to assign a single or predominant swimming behaviour.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on in vivo observations.

claim: In vessels with a normal blood flow and in the presence of red blood cells, trypanosomes were dragged passively by the flow along with red blood cells.
source: In vessels with a normal blood flow and in the presence of red blood cells, trypanosomes were dragged passively by the flow along with red blood cells.
evidence: This is a direct observation from in vivo imaging.

claim: In the centre of large vessels, the velocity of the flow does not allow either tumbling or directional swimming against or faster than the flow.
source: In the centre of large vessels, such as the cardinal artery or cardinal vein, the velocity of the flow does not allow either tumbling or directional swimming against or faster than the flow.
evidence: This is an inference based on observations of trypanosome behavior in large vessels.

claim: In narrow ISCs, trypanosomes are forced to move forward because of streaming of the blood or the presence of colliding red blood cells.
source: Similarly, in narrow iISCs, trypanosomes are forced to move forward because of streaming of the blood or the presence of colliding red blood cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on observations in ISCs.

claim: Under conditions with normal blood flow and red blood cells, trypanosomes were never seen swimming faster than the passive movement of red blood cells.
source: Under these conditions, trypanosomes were never seen swimming faster than the passive movement of red blood cells as previously suggested (Heddergott et al., 2012; Langousis and Hill, 2014).
evidence: This is a direct observation that contradicts previous suggestions in the literature.

claim: Because trypanosomes are carried along with red blood cells by the flow, it is difficult to envisage how the red blood cells could represent anything more than very occasional obstacles or surfaces for mechanical interactions.
source: Furthermore, because trypanosomes are carried along with red blood cells by the flow, it is difficult to envisage how the red blood cells could represent anything more than very occasional obstacles or surfaces for mechanical interactions that would favour forward swimming (Bargul et al., 2016; Heddergott et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on observations that challenges previous hypotheses.

claim: At the periphery of the cardinal vein, there is a cell-free layer where the number of red blood cells and the speed of the blood flow is reduced.
source: At the periphery of the cardinal vein, there is a cell-free layer where the number of red blood cells and the speed of the blood flow is reduced (Bagchi, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bagchi, 2007.

claim: In the cell-free layer, trypanosomes could clearly slow themselves down by crawling, rolling or by temporarily anchoring themselves to the dorsal endothelium.
source: Here, trypanosomes could clearly slow themselves down by crawling, rolling or by temporarily anchoring themselves to the dorsal endothelium (further discussed below).
evidence: This is a direct observation from in vivo imaging.

claim: In arteries or small capillaries, adherence to the epithelium was never observed, even when the flow was reduced or completely absent.
source: However, in arteries or small capillaries, adherence to the epithelium was never observed, even when the flow was reduced or completely absent.
evidence: This is a direct observation about where adherence does not occur.

claim: Not only the velocity of the flow but also the type of endothelium influences trypanosome swimming behaviour.
source: This suggests that not only the velocity of the flow but also the type of endothelium influences trypanosome swimming behaviour.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that adherence is vessel-type specific.

claim: Physiological changes occur as the infection progresses that modify conditions within blood vessels.
source: Physiological changes occur as the infection progresses that modify conditions within blood vessels.
evidence: This is a general observation about infection-related changes.

claim: The flow is strongly reduced or interrupted and the density of red blood cells is reduced by obstruction of blood vessels or anaemia.
source: The flow is strongly reduced or interrupted and the density of red blood cells is reduced by obstruction of blood vessels or anaemia.
evidence: This is a direct observation of physiological changes during infection.

claim: In conditions where flow is reduced and red blood cells are reduced, directional swimmers were observed that swam faster than the flow and others that swam against the flow, or that repeatedly changed direction within blood vessels.
source: In these conditions, directional swimmers were observed that swam faster than the flow and others that swam against the flow, or that repeatedly changed direction within blood vessels (Video 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Video 4.

claim: It is not possible to generalize the swimming behaviour of trypanosomes in blood as they can rapidly adopt different swimming behaviours: tumbling, directional swimming or anchoring.
source: Taken together, our observations show that it is not possible to generalize the swimming behaviour of trypanosomes in blood as they can rapidly adopt different swimming behaviours: tumbling, directional swimming or anchoring.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on comprehensive in vivo observations.

claim: These behaviours are all largely influenced by the size and type of vessel, the speed of the flow, the presence, or not, of red blood cells as well as the highly dynamic microenvironment within a vessel.
source: These behaviours are all largely influenced by the size and type of vessel, the speed of the flow, the presence, or not, of red blood cells as well as the highly dynamic microenvironment within a vessel, for example the centre compared to the periphery, and the type of endothelium.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion about factors influencing swimming behavior.

claim: It has been suggested that the directionality of swimming is influenced by the density or compactness of the tissue.
source: Outside of the blood, it has been suggested that the directionality of swimming is influenced by the density or compactness of the tissue (Bargul et al., 2016; Sun et al., 2018; Wheeler et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Observation of swimming behaviour in various tissues revealed that it is the size of the interstitial space through which the trypanosome has to swim that largely determines whether it will swim directionally, tumble or both.
source: Our observation of swimming behaviour in various tissues revealed that it is the size of the interstitial space through which the trypanosome has to swim that largely determines whether it will swim directionally, tumble or both.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on observations in various tissue types.

claim: Within the compact tissue of the fins, where the space below epithelial cells is very narrow and the basement membrane is not deformable, the vast majority of trypanosomes swim directionally.
source: For example, within the compact tissue of the fins, where the space below epithelial cells is very narrow (mesenchyme) and the basement membrane is not deformable (Mateus et al., 2012), the vast majority of trypanosomes swim directionally.
evidence: This claim is supported by observations and a citation about fin tissue structure.

claim: This observation is in agreement with the swimming behaviour described for procyclic forms of T. brucei swimming through microfluidic devices smaller than their maximum cell diameter.
source: This observation is in agreement with the swimming behaviour described for procyclic forms of T. brucei swimming through microfluidic devices smaller than their maximum cell diameter, mimicking potential size-limiting environments within host tissues (Sun et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a comparison with findings from a cited study.

claim: In zebrafish fins, the space can be so restrictive that to invert direction the trypanosome is obliged to swim backwards.
source: In zebrafish fins, the space can be so restrictive that to invert direction the trypanosome is obliged to swim backwards (Video 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations shown in Video 7.

claim: Trypanosomes can adopt several swimming behaviours and these are largely influenced by the compactness and confinement offered by the tissue.
source: Altogether, these observations indicate that trypanosomes can adopt several swimming behaviours and that these are largely influenced by the compactness and confinement offered by the tissue.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion about factors influencing swimming behavior in tissues.

claim: One of the most interesting observations is the discovery that trypanosomes can anchor themselves to the vein endothelium by their posterior end, leaving the flagellum and the entire cell body free to move.
source: Perhaps one of the most interesting observations is the discovery that trypanosomes can anchor themselves to the vein endothelium by their posterior end, leaving the flagellum and the entire cell body free to move.
evidence: This is a primary novel finding of the study.

claim: Anchoring was observed as soon as 30 min to 1 h after T. carassii injection into zebrafish larvae.
source: Anchoring was observed as soon as 30 min to 1 h after T. carassii injection into zebrafish larvae
evidence: This is a direct observation about the timing of anchoring.

claim: By 1 dpi extravasation was observed.
source: and by 1 dpi extravasation was observed.
evidence: This is a direct observation about the timing of extravasation.

claim: Under the current conditions, it was not possible to ascertain whether this adhesion mechanism favours or is even required for extravasation.
source: Under the current conditions, it was not possible to ascertain whether this adhesion mechanism favours or is even required for extravasation.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation of the current study.

claim: The anchoring site on the posterior of the trypanosome leaves the cell body and flagellum free to move, so it seems likely that the adhesion on the trypanosome occurs via the flagellum base or the neck of the flagellar pocket itself.
source: The anchoring site on the posterior of the trypanosome leaves the cell body and flagellum free to move (Video 2 and Video 5), so it seems likely that the adhesion on the trypanosome occurs via the flagellum base or the neck of the flagellar pocket itself.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that the flagellum remains free to move.

claim: The presence of specific adhesion molecules would at least partly explain how T. carassii can very rapidly anchor themselves upon sudden collision with the endothelium.
source: The presence of specific adhesion molecules would at least partly explain how T. carassii can very rapidly anchor themselves, upon sudden collision with the endothelium, and remain in position for more than 15 s despite the very rapid blood flow and collisions with blood cells.
evidence: This is speculation about the molecular mechanism of anchoring.

claim: Anchoring was only observed in the cardinal vein but trypanosomes were seen crawling on vein endothelium through dynamic interactions that involved the cell membrane, not just the flagellum membrane.
source: Anchoring was only observed in the cardinal vein but trypanosomes were seen crawling on vein endothelium (Video 5) through dynamic interactions that involved the cell membrane, not just the flagellum membrane
evidence: This is a direct observation comparing anchoring and crawling behaviors.

claim: The molecules required for whole-cell adherence might be different from those required for anchoring through the posterior end.
source: suggesting that the molecules required for whole-cell adherence might be different from those required for anchoring through the posterior end.
evidence: This is speculation based on the different types of attachment observed.

claim: Anchoring is reminiscent of leukocyte rolling, which also occurs only in veins and not in arteries.
source: This is reminiscent of leukocyte rolling, which also occurs only in veins and not in arteries.
evidence: This is a comparison with a known biological phenomenon.

claim: The possibility to observe T. carassii behaviour both in vitro and in vivo, in the presence or absence of a strong hydrodynamic flow, and at various locations within the vertebrate host, demonstrated how the environmental conditions, especially the presence or absence of a flow, strongly influence the ability of the trypanosome to attach and the duration of the attachment.
source: Altogether, the possibility to observe T. carassii behaviour both in vitro and in vivo, in the presence or absence of a strong hydrodynamic flow, and at various locations within the vertebrate host, demonstrated how the environmental conditions, especially the presence or absence of a flow, strongly influence the ability of the trypanosome to attach and the duration of the attachment.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion about factors influencing attachment.

claim: T. carassii anchors to zebrafish cells in a manner clearly distinct from that described for other trypanosomes.
source: T. carassii anchors to zebrafish cells in a manner clearly distinct from that described for other trypanosomes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparison with attachment mechanisms in other trypanosomes.

claim: The major difference is the lack of extensive interaction between the trypanosome's flagellum membrane and the host cell or artificial surface.
source: The major difference being the lack of extensive interaction between the trypanosome's flagellum membrane and the host cell or artificial surface.
evidence: This is a comparison with attachment mechanisms described for other trypanosomes.

claim: Stable interaction involving large portions of the flagellum membrane has been described for haptomonads stages of Paratrypanosoma confusum, or Leishmania promastigotes.
source: Stable interaction involving large portions of the flagellum membrane has been described among others for haptomonads stages (surface-attached) of Paratrypanosoma confusum, or Leishmania promastigotes (Figure 11A) (Skalický et al., 2017; Wakid and Bates, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies describing attachment in other parasites.

claim: In liberiform parasites, adhesion occurs through an attachment pad forming from the bulge at the base of the flagellum.
source: In these liberform parasites (flagellum not laterally attached to the cell), adhesion occurs through an attachment pad forming from the bulge at the base of the flagellum.
evidence: This is established knowledge about attachment in liberiform parasites.

claim: At least in vitro, the formation of the pad takes approximately 1 h, causing extensive remodelling of the flagellum itself.
source: At least in vitro, the formation of the pad takes approximately 1 h, causing extensive remodelling of the flagellum itself, and effectively anchors the parasites to the surface, and in the case of P. confusum, also favours their division (Skalický et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Skalický et al., 2017.

claim: T. brucei epimastigotes divide while attached to the brush border of the salivary gland epithelium through extensive outgrowths of the non-cell-attached anterior part of the flagellum membrane.
source: Similarly, T. brucei epimastigotes divide while attached to the brush border of the salivary gland epithelium through extensive outgrowths of the non-cell-attached anterior part of the flagellum membrane (Figure 11B) (Beattie and Gull, 1997; Langousis and Hill, 2014; Schuster et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: T. congolense was reported to adhere in vitro to bovine aorta endothelial (BAE) cell monolayers via extensive membrane protrusions (filopodia) of the membrane-attached flagellum.
source: T. congolense was reported to adhere in vitro to bovine aorta endothelial (BAE) cell monolayers via extensive membrane protrusions (filopodia) of the membrane-attached flagellum (Figure 11C) (Beattie and Gull, 1997; Hemphill and Ross, 1995)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on T. congolense attachment.

claim: T. congolense interaction with BAE cells was shown to involve sialic acid residues on BAE cells.
source: an interaction that was shown to involve sialic acid residues on BAE cells (Hemphill et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hemphill et al., 1994.

claim: Although adhesion of T. congolense was observed already at 1 h, the filopodia increased in size over a period of 24–48 h.
source: Although adhesion was observed already at 1 h, the filopodia increased in size over a period of 24–48 h.
evidence: This is information from previous studies about the kinetics of T. congolense attachment.

claim: Whether such a type of interaction occurs with similar kinetics also in vivo, in vessels with an intact blood flow, is yet to be confirmed.
source: Whether such a type of interaction occurs with similar kinetics also in vivo, in vessels with an intact blood flow, is yet to be confirmed.
evidence: This is speculation about whether in vitro observations apply in vivo.

claim: All the attachment mechanisms described for other trypanosomes are clearly geared towards creating a very stable interaction with a surface.
source: All the above attachment mechanisms are clearly geared towards creating a very stable interaction with a surface to either establish a permanent infection in the salivary glands of the insect host, or to possibly adhere to the vertebrate host endothelium.
evidence: This is an inference about the function of attachment mechanisms in other trypanosomes.

claim: Most of the interactions described for other trypanosomes were observed in vitro for trypanosomes cultivated on glass or plastic surfaces or endothelial cell monolayers and studied by means of scanning or transmission electron microscopy.
source: Most of these interactions, however, were observed in vitro for (para)trypanosomes cultivated on glass or plastic surfaces or endothelial cell monolayers and studied by means of scanning or transmission electron microscopy, as well as in vitro binding assays (Beattie and Gull, 1997; Hemphill and Ross, 1995; Hemphill et al., 1994; Skalický et al., 2017; Vickerman, 1969; Wakid and Bates, 2004).
evidence: This is a summary of the methodologies used in previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: To what extent the kinetics of interaction and the size of the contact area described for other trypanosomes also apply to the more dynamic in vivo environment is yet to be ascertained.
source: Therefore, to what extent the kinetics of interaction and the size of the contact area described also apply to the more dynamic in vivo environment is yet to be ascertained.
evidence: This is speculation about the applicability of in vitro findings to in vivo conditions.

claim: The interactions between T. carassii and zebrafish cells were limited to the tip of the posterior end of the trypanosome body, leaving the entire flagellum and trypanosome cell body free to rapidly move.
source: The interactions between T. carassii and zebrafish cells were limited to the tip of the posterior end of the trypanosome body (Figure 11D), leaving the entire flagellum and trypanosome cell body free to rapidly move (Video 2).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the study.

claim: Despite the small surface involved, anchoring occurred very rapidly, suggesting a very strong, yet dynamic, type of interaction.
source: Despite the small surface involved, anchoring occurred very rapidly, suggesting a very strong, yet dynamic, type of interaction
evidence: This is an inference based on the rapid nature of anchoring.

claim: The duration of anchoring was influenced by the presence or absence of a strong hydrodynamic flow as well as colliding red blood cells.
source: the duration of which was influenced by the presence or absence of a strong hydrodynamic flow as well as colliding red blood cells.
evidence: This is a direct observation about factors affecting anchoring duration.

claim: Given the in vivo dynamic conditions within a blood vessel, it seems unlikely that T. carassii would establish stable interactions that involve large portions of the trypanosome cell surface, as for example described in vitro for T. congolense.
source: Given the in vivo dynamic conditions within a blood vessel, it seems unlikely that T. carassii would establish stable interactions that involve large portions of the trypanosome cell surface, as for example described in vitro for T. congolense.
evidence: This is speculation based on the dynamic nature of the in vivo environment.

claim: Because T. carassii adherence to red blood cells and to glass surfaces was also observed in vitro, it will be possible to investigate the adhesion mechanism at high resolution in the future.
source: Nevertheless, because T. carassii adherence to red blood cells and to glass surfaces was also observed in vitro, it will be possible to investigate the adhesion mechanism at high resolution in the future.
evidence: This is speculation about future research possibilities.

claim: This is the first description of the swimming behaviour of a trypanosome in vivo in the natural environment of a vertebrate host.
source: In conclusion, we describe here for the first time the swimming behaviour of a trypanosome in vivo in the natural environment of a vertebrate host.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the work.

claim: The study reports the complex and heterogeneous environment in which the trypanosomes reside and how this highly influences the swimming behaviour.
source: We report the complex and heterogeneous environment in which the trypanosomes reside and how this highly influences the swimming behaviour.
evidence: This is a summary of a primary finding of the study.

claim: It is not possible to assign specific behaviours to trypanosomes swimming in any of the host compartments, as the trypanosomes were extremely effective in rapidly adapting their motion to the highly dynamic host environment.
source: We describe how it is not possible to assign specific behaviours to trypanosomes swimming in any of the host compartments, as the trypanosomes were extremely effective in rapidly adapting their motion to the highly dynamic host environment.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study.

claim: The study describes backward swimming and whip-like movements that allowed trypanosomes to invert direction.
source: We describe backward swimming and whip-like movements that allowed trypanosomes to invert direction
evidence: This is a summary of novel behaviors observed in the study.

claim: The study identified the posterior end as a novel anchoring site that allows the cell to adhere to host cells in a manner different from those described to date for other trypanosomes.
source: as well as identifiedying the posterior end as a novel anchoring site that allows the cell to adhere to host cells in a manner different from those described to date for other trypanosomes.
evidence: This is a summary of a primary novel finding.

claim: Establishment of the T. carassii zebrafish infection model in combination with the genetic tractability of the zebrafish and of trypanosomes, represent a unique possibility to address questions related to trypanosome biology and host-pathogen interaction.
source: Altogether, establishment of the T. carassii zebrafish infection model in combination with the genetic tractability of the zebrafish and of trypanosomes, represent a unique possibility to address questions related to: 1) trypanosome swimming behaviour in vivo in the natural environment of a vertebrate host, 2) host-pathogen interaction, 3) trypanosome biology, 4) the effect of specific immune factors on the progression of the infection, 5) the effect of drugs on both the trypanosome and the host, and 6) immune evasion strategies of trypanosomes that do not present antigenic variation.
evidence: This is speculation about the future applications of the model.

claim: The T. carassii-zebrafish model holds the promise to become a valuable complementary model to those currently available, to study the complex biology of trypanosomes and their interaction with the vertebrate host.
source: For all these reasons, the T. carassii-zebrafish model holds the promise to become a valuable complementary model to those currently available, to study the complex biology of trypanosomes and their interaction with the vertebrate host.
evidence: This is speculation about the future value of the model.
